items.item: A destructor is two parts: the type's own Drop::drop (if any), then compiler-generated drop glue that recursively drops every field. A struct with no Drop impl still drops its fields, so most types never need impl Drop; only types that directly manage a resource do.

at.deep: The destructor, as the Reference states it

items.item: Aggregates drop front to back: struct fields in declaration order, tuple elements in order, the active enum variant's fields in declaration order, array/owned-slice elements first to last; the outer Drop::drop runs before any field is dropped. The order in which a closure's move-captures drop is unspecified.

at.deep: Every drop-order rule, with a trace

items.item: Locals drop back to front: on leaving a drop scope, variables drop in reverse declaration order and temporaries in reverse creation order; when several scopes are left at once (return) they unwind inside-out; function parameters are in the outermost scope and drop last, each after the bindings made by its own pattern.

at.deep: Every drop-order rule, with a trace

items.item: Bindings in one pattern (let (a, b) = ...) drop in reverse declaration order, and for or-patterns the order is fixed by the first sub-pattern even when a later alternative matched.

items.item: A temporary lives until the end of its temporary scope, usually the enclosing statement, so `m.lock().unwrap().push(x);` releases the lock at the semicolon. The scrutinee of a match is not a temporary scope, so a guard created there lives until the end of the whole statement, which is the classic way to hold a lock too long by accident. If-conditions, lazy && / || operands and match guards each get their own narrower scope.

items.item: Temporary lifetime extension: in `let x = &temp();` (and through tuple, struct, array, cast, braced-block tail, if/else and match-arm operands) the temporary lives to the end of the block. Function-call arguments, method receivers, match scrutinees, closure/async bodies and break operands are not extending, so `let x = identity(&temp());` does not compile.

items.item: When an expression is abandoned part-way through (break, return, ? or panic inside an operand), the operand temporaries already created drop in reverse creation order; operands never evaluated are never created.

items.item: Rust 2024 if-let rescoping: temporaries in an `if let` scrutinee now drop before the else block (previously they lived to the end of the whole if-let), which fixes the `if let Some(x) = *lock.read().unwrap() { .. } else { lock.write() }` self-deadlock. Rewriting it as `match` restores the old, longer lifetime; the if_let_rescope lint flags affected code during `cargo fix --edition`.

items.item: `let _ = expr;` vs `let _g = expr;`: the wildcard `_` does not bind, move or borrow, so a guard returned by `let _ = mutex.lock();` is a temporary dropped at once and the lock is released immediately, while `_g` binds and holds the guard (MutexGuard: the lock is released when the guard is dropped) until the end of scope.

items.item: The model RAII wrapper for an OS resource is OwnedFd (OwnedHandle on Windows). It closes the descriptor on drop and guarantees that nobody else will close it. It is repr(transparent) and never -1, so it can cross FFI as an owned argument or return value, and as_fd lends a BorrowedFd without giving up ownership.

at.deep: RAII in Rust against defer, with, try-with-resources and C++

items.item: Closing exactly once is enforced by ownership, not by runtime checks. The wrapper is not Copy or Clone (duplication goes through try_clone, which makes a new descriptor). from_raw_fd is unsafe because the caller must hand over an open descriptor fit to be owned that needs no cleanup other than close. into_raw_fd gives up ownership, so drop no longer closes it.

at.quote: into_raw_fd(self)/from_raw_fd are the explicit ownership handoffs that prevent use-after-close

items.item: I/O safety: a descriptor is owned or borrowed much like memory. A safe fn that takes a plain integer and acts on it as a descriptor is unsound, because closing a descriptor you do not own lets the number be reused, and the real owner then works on the wrong file (misbehavior, possibly UB).

Drop cannot report failure: File's Drop ignores errors detected on close. Where those errors matter, call an explicit fallible method (sync_all, or a consuming close/finish method on your own wrapper) and keep Drop as the best-effort fallback.

items.item: mem::forget is a safe fn because Rust's safety guarantees do not include destructors always running (Rc cycles and process::exit already skip them). So any unsafe code must allow for it: you cannot return a value and rely on the caller running its destructor.

Prefer ManuallyDrop over forget when handing ownership to raw parts (Vec -> from_raw_parts). With forget, a panic between taking the raw parts and the forget call double-frees, and passing the now-invalid value to forget is itself UB; wrapping in ManuallyDrop first removes both problems.

items.item: ManuallyDrop<T> is zero-cost and has the same layout and validity as T (not a substitute for MaybeUninit). Reading the inner value is safe, so ManuallyDrop::drop is unsafe and a dropped value must never be reachable through a safe public API. Even #[derive(Debug/Clone/PartialEq/Hash)] on a struct holding one can be unsound.

items.item: The leakpocalypse (2015): thread::scoped returned a JoinGuard whose Drop joined the child thread, and soundness depended on that Drop always running. An Rc cycle could leak the guard in safe code, so the child could use the parent's freed stack (issue #24292). RFC 1066 then made mem::forget safe just before 1.0 and stated that not running destructors is not unsafe.

Leaks matter for soundness mainly in proxy types, which manage access to data they do not own (vec::Drain, Rc, the old JoinGuard). Unsafe code cannot rely on destructors running in order to be safe; safe application code may treat a leak as a bug.

items.item: Leak amplification ('pre-pooping your pants'): put the owner into a trivially safe state before handing out the proxy, and let Drop restore the good state. Vec::drain sets len to 0 up front, so a forgotten Drain only leaks more elements (std documents that the vector may lose elements arbitrarily) rather than exposing freed memory.

items.item: Forget can also break counting invariants: forgetting Rc clones can overflow the refcount and cause a use-after-free, so std aborts on refcount overflow instead of assuming the count matches the live handles.

at.deep: Proxy types and leak amplification

items.item: The leak-proof redesign is std::thread::scope (1.63). The guarantee lives in a closure-taking function that joins every unjoined thread before it returns, not in a guard's Drop, so leaking a scoped thread handle cannot break it. The 'scope / 'env lifetimes express the borrow. Caveat: the join waits only for each thread's main function, not its thread-local destructors.

items.item: Gankra's ranking of how much a type can rely on its destructor: no destructor; leaking just wastes resources; leaking skips other destructors; and 'leaves the world in an unexpected but safe state'. Push reliance as high up this list as practical; anything worse than the last, i.e. relying on Drop for memory safety, is forbidden in an API that claims to be safe.

items.item: Pin's Drop guarantee is the one place Drop interacts with soundness: the memory of a pinned !Unpin value must not be invalidated or reused until its drop has run. Leaking it (never freeing the memory) is still allowed; freeing or reusing the memory without dropping is not. Custom storage must call ptr::drop_in_place before reuse.

items.item: Manual destruction in custom containers and smart pointers goes through ptr::drop_in_place. It is required for unsized values and lets you drop pinned data; the pointer must be valid for reads and writes and aligned (packed fields must be copied out first), and the pointee counts as dropped afterwards.

items.item: Edition 2021 disjoint closure captures change drop timing: a move closure that uses only t.0 now captures and drops only t.0 when the closure drops, while the rest of t drops at t's own scope end. The edition migration flags closures whose capture changes affect drop order.

at.out: Closure capture rules and their drop timing are not in Chapter 1 (CHAPTER.md A.7 defers closures to Chapter 2 section 2.2); the Deep dive notes that closure move-captures drop in an unspecified order.
